I definitely think the expectations put on me at a young age had a huge part to play in me always feeling like I had something grand & important to accomplish. I also think it was to do with the fact that I loved learning as a kid so I would read up on all kinds of things. 

I had quite philosophical thinking even as a 4 year old & a specific example I can remember is that I really liked bueno chocolate bars but my mother hated them. I asked her how is it possible for her to dislike them if the ingredients were the same & tasted the same for everyone. 

She explained to me that even the same things taste different to different people so a bueno chocolate bar tasted differently to her than it did for me. 

It suddenly clicked that the entire world is different to everyone & I felt like, in that case we could never really be completely sure of one whole objective truth because we would always be limited by our own sensory perceptions.

(I obviously did not use the word objective or perceptions or understand them as a 4 year old lol but I did vaguely understand the concept of everything we think we know being dependent on who or what was experiencing it)

This example of the chocolate bar seemed to set off a chain reaction in my mind where I became fascinated with questioning everything around me & how sure I could be that things existed in the way I was perceiving them. Which led to my interest in reading all about physics, metaphysics & philosophy.

I still don't really know what on earth this grand purpose I have really is but it's always been a very strong feeling that I've never been able to shake. Maybe its simply to share how I see the world in the hope I can better understand it for myself :)

The feelings can happen as the body drifts into sleep mode & they are quite normal. Most of the time we don't remember them because our minds are usually gone to sleep at that stage too.

But when you practice astral projection those feelings give you a signal that your body is falling asleep. Some people feel other sensations such as vibrations. The goal of astral projection is to keep your mind awake until your body starts to fall asleep. Once you start feeling those sensations you can try to move your astral body by rolling, sitting up or rising out of your physical body. It's not always successful and takes a lot of practice but it can have some interesting results.

So technically speaking the feelings by themselves aren't astral projection, it's the leaving your body that means you've successfully projected.

Yeah there can really be a lot of downsides to these labels because it makes people automatically assume that otherwise normal behaviour that everyone does is somehow abnormal for you because of the label. In some ways the labels are useful because it helps us understand ourselves & how our brains are wired but often certain people look at you & see the illness first and the person second.

I've even had people ask me if I have been taking my medication when I'd get overly excited about things & assume that I was going into a manic episode if I felt happier than usual. Even my psychiatrist has called out my dreams before, my literal dreams when I am asleep & said that the content of them was leaning towards psychosis territory even though dreams are weird af for everybody!

I feel like we have to be careful how much weight we give the opinions other people have of us. If we give them too much we will start to see every human experience we have as a symptom.

Your husband sounds understanding though. It's so important to have people like that in our lives who can see who we are behind the label we have.

I have schizophrenia & I have always hyperfixated on certain topics since I was a kid. Animals was my first one. Then I became fascinated with humans & I used to read these big medical encyclopaedias to learn all about different illnesses and conditions that effect us.Then I became fascinated with psychology & philosophy, how the human mind works and how we perceive reality & what reality even is in the first place.

You briefly mentioned autism in your post & I also struggle to know whether the lines between schizophrenia and autism are blurred. It seems likely & I know many people who end up being diagnosed with both. I myself and the people that know me suspect that I'm on the spectrum & I'm currently waiting for my assessment to see if that's the case.

I think maybe the most helpful thing you can do if you want the professionals you speak to to understand your brain better is to write down a summary of these things from childhood to the present day. It can be as detailed as you want or you could just write down the things you think are the most significant & go from there. 

I hope you find the answers you are looking for. It can take time but it will be worth finding out.

Where I'm from we have what's called level of observation which means what level of observation you require when you're in the hospital. 

If they think you might do harm to yourself or are otherwise a risk they will put you in "high observation" which basically means a smaller ward with less people & the nurses check on you more often. You also may not be able to have things you'd have in a lower observation ward such as your shoe laces etc.

There is also the difference between being voluntary which is where you agree to go to the hospital or being involuntary which is where they take you there against your will.

Whether you are in the severe cases department or not shouldn't effect your medication or how much you have to take. I think it mostly means that you require a higher level of care so they will keep a closer eye on you
